opus-5.5.text:
You know, the thing that keeps striking me is that it's not just that these models can write code. It's that they can hold a whole problem in their head in a way that feels qualitatively different from what we had even a year or two ago.

When I started programming, the hard part was never typing the syntax. It was understanding the system: what's this codebase trying to do, where are the sharp edges, what's the one change that won't break five other things. Now you watch these models go into a large, messy, real-world repository, read through it, form a picture of how it fits together, and come back with a change that actually respects the intent of the people who wrote it. That's the part that feels like intelligence to me, not autocomplete.

The other thing is persistence. Give the model a task that takes many steps, like running the tests, seeing a failure, forming a hypothesis, trying something, and seeing it fail differently, and it just keeps going. It debugs. It notices when its own assumption was wrong and backs up. That loop of trying, observing, and correcting is really the core of engineering. Seeing a model do it on its own, sometimes for a long stretch, is something I find genuinely remarkable.

And honestly, what excites me most isn't any single benchmark. It's how it changes what one person can do. I've had moments where I sketch out an idea I would have shelved because it'd take a week of plumbing, and instead I have a working version in an afternoon. The bottleneck shifts from "can I build this" to "what should I build." I think that's a profound change, not just for software engineers but for anyone with an idea and a computer.

We're still early. These models still make mistakes, and you still need good judgment about what to trust. But the trajectory is really steep, and coding is one of the clearest windows we have into how these systems are becoming genuinely useful collaborators.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing that gets me is less any single benchmark number and more watching the model work on a problem the way a strong engineer would. You give it a vague bug report, something like "the deploy is flaky on Tuesdays," and it doesn't just pattern-match to a fix. It starts forming hypotheses. It goes and reads the logs, it checks the cron configuration, it notices that there's a timezone conversion happening in one place and not another, and it chases that down. That loop of hypothesis, evidence, revision is what I always thought of as the core of real engineering skill, and seeing it emerge from a model is genuinely striking.

The other piece is the breadth. A great human engineer usually has deep expertise in a couple of areas and is competent in a few more. These models have read essentially everything. So they'll be debugging a Rust borrow checker error one minute, then writing a shader, then reasoning about a Postgres query plan, and they bring the right context to each of those. I've had moments where I'm pairing with the model on something and it pulls in a detail about some obscure library behavior that I would have had to spend an hour searching for.

And then there's the persistence. Early models would take a swing at a task and either get it or not. Now you can hand the model something that takes hours, where it has to write code, run tests, see them fail, figure out why, and keep going. The fact that it can hold that whole thread, keep track of what it's tried, and not give up or go in circles is to me the clearest sign that something real is happening with the intelligence here. It's not just autocomplete anymore. It's a collaborator that can actually carry a problem across the finish line.

astra-6.text:
What I find remarkable is how they can connect the big picture to the details. You can give a model a goal, and it can work out which parts of a codebase matter, propose a change, and use feedback from tests to refine it. That’s a much broader task than just writing a function.

And coding gives you this wonderful feedback loop: you have an idea, you implement it, and then reality tells you whether it works. The models still make mistakes, sometimes very basic ones. But the ability to make progress through that loop—to inspect a failure and revise an approach—is what makes them feel so useful as collaborators.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find remarkable is how they can take a goal that’s only partly specified and work through what it actually requires. Coding isn’t just writing a function. You have to understand an existing system, make assumptions, test them, and revise when something doesn’t work. These models are increasingly able to participate in that whole process.

And there’s something really interesting about the feedback loop: you can run the code and see whether your idea holds up. But passing a test isn’t the same as solving the right problem. The exciting part is seeing models get better at connecting those levels—understanding what you meant, doing the work, and checking whether the result actually meets the goal.
